text.p: By Dr Heinz Grimm, director of the economics division, Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG

Foreign direct investment in Germany fell dramatically last year. According to the Bundesbank's calculations, foreign investment in Germany swung from plus 17 billion marks ($9.9 billion) to minus five billion, which means that foreign investors actually withdrew money from Germany on a net basis. Since German companies at the same time continued to invest strongly abroad, capital export continued to rise in the balance of direct investment, a trend which continued in the first months of this year: In the first quarter of 1997, capital outflow rose nearly 30 percent to 14.1 billion marks compared with the previous year.

For some observers, this development is further proof of Germany's inadequacy as a business location. Disadvantageous conditions such as high wage costs, for example, or taxes and other contributions which are excessive on an international scale, as well as crippling state regulation, are said to cause investment capital to, increasingly, pass Germany by. Of course this interpretation is not easy to dismiss out of hand in light of the fact that the environment in Germany is clearly not favourable for investments. However on closer scrutiny it does not prove valid.

It is forgotten all too quickly, for example, that a stream of major foreign investments sharply distorted the result on balance in 1995. After foreign investors spent a net 20 billion marks in Germany between 1990 and 1994, the 1995 investment volume surged to more than 17 billion. Viewed in this way, the recent capital drain primarily signals a normalisation of foreign spending, of which the average of the past two years (6.2 billion marks) still significantly exceeds the average from 1990 to 1996 (4.7 billion).

A more detailed look at individual underlying statistics on the balance of direct investments also supports the theory that the investment decline is not only attributable to the prevailing operating conditions. The capital drain is primarily the result of profit-taking and the redemption of long term loans. It appears that many foreign firms used the favourable earnings developments at their German subsidiaries to pay off long term credit lines and did not reinvest profit in Germany last year. At the same time the breadth of new investments, at 24 billion marks (even if it was outstripped in 1996 by withdrawals) leads one to conclude that there are still attractive investment opportunities for foreign investors.

As well as this, the significance of the capital drain associated with direct investment should not be overstated. From an economic perspective, swings in the volume of foreign investors' net deposits have no significant consequences. With an average of around five billion marks, barely five percent of Germany's annual investment volume comes from foreign investors. And on the other hand there can be no question of a flight of capital: only about one tenth of investment by German companies goes abroad and it is an accepted fact that this is primarily to secure and extend companies' positions in important export markets.

And finally there is no basis, even on an international comparison, for the theory that the balance of direct investments reflects the competitiveness of a location. According to the latest ratings by the Geneva-based World Economic Forum, the weighting of foreign direct invesment among the world's 20 most competitive nations varies between eight percent of gross domestic product (Singapore) and zero percent (Japan). Neither can one draw any direct conclusions from the balance of direct investments. This ranges among the top 20 from plus six percent of GDP (Malaysia) and minus three percent (Switzerland).

All in all, there is scarcely any doubt that structural reforms are urgently needed to improve the investment climate in Germany. However, the decline in foreign direct investment that is so often bemoaned in this context is no cause for concern at the present time.
(The opinions expressed represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.) ($ = 1.725 German Marks)
